records.title: A disproportionate role for the fornix and mammillary bodies in recall versus recognition memory
Memory-Based Advertising Effectiveness Techniques: Recall versus Recognition
Visual Memory in Unilateral Spatial Neglect: Immediate Recall versus Delayed Recognition
records.abstract: Patients with unilateral spatial neglect (USN) often show impaired performance in spatial working memory tasks, apart from the difficulty retrieving "left-sided" spatial data from long-term memory, shown in the "piazza effect" by Bisiach and colleagues. This study's aim was to compare the effect of the spatial position of a visual object on immediate and delayed memory performance in USN patients. Specifically, immediate verbal recall performance, tested using a simultaneous presentation of four visual objects in four quadrants, was compared with memory in a later-provided recognition task, in which objects were individually shown at the screen center. Unlike healthy controls, USN patients showed a left-side disadvantage and a vertical bias in the immediate free recall task (69% vs. 42% recall for right- and left-sided objects, respectively). In the recognition task, the patients correctly recognized half of "old" items, and their correct rejection rate was 95.5%. Importantly, when the analysis focused on previously recalled items (in the immediate task), no statistically significant difference was found in the delayed recognition of objects according to their original quadrant of presentation. Furthermore, USN patients were able to recollect the correct original location of the recognized objects in 60% of the cases, well beyond chance level. This suggests that the memory trace formed in these cases was not only semantic but also contained a visuospatial tag. Finally, successful recognition of objects missed in recall trials points to formation of memory traces for neglected contralesional objects, which may become accessible to retrieval processes in explicit memory.

records.title: Effects of repeated collaborative retrieval on individual memory vary as a function of recall versus recognition tasks
records.abstract: Our research examines how prior group collaboration modulates later individual memory. We recently showed that repeated collaborative recall sessions benefit later individual recall more than a single collaborative recall session (Blumen & Rajaram, 2008). Current research compared the effects of repeated collaborative recall and repeated collaborative recognition on later individual recall and later individual recognition. A total of 192 participants studied a list of nouns and then completed three successive retrieval sessions in one of four conditions. While two collaborative recall sessions and two collaborative recognition sessions generated comparable levels of individual recall (CRecall-CRecall-I Recall approximately CRecognition-CRecognition-I Recall , Experiment 1a), two collaborative recognition sessions generated greater levels of individual recognition than two collaborative recall sessions (CRecognition-CRecognition- IRecognition > CRecall-CRecall- I Recognition , Experiment 1b). These findings are discussed in terms of two opposing mechanisms that operate during collaborative retrieval-re-exposure and retrieval disruption-and in terms of transfer-appropriate processing across collaborative and individual retrieval sessions.

records.title: Children's Memory for Picture versus Word Responses in Paired Associates: Recall and Recognition Tests
records.abstract: The 96 second-graders each had three study/test trials with picture/picture or picture/word associates. With a recall test, the traditional finding that word responses are better recalled was replicated; with a four-alternative recognition task, there was no difference in retention of picture or word responses (except on the first trial, where pictures were superior to words); and with a modified recognition test, picture responses were better recalled. Children apparently do have difficulty decoding visual images to verbal representations, but the nature of the memory task itself is a critical factor in tests of that effect.

records.title: Free recall versus combined cued recall and recognition to detect true memory impairment on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment
records.abstract: Background The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) is widely used as a brief screening measure to characterize overall cognitive status. Although only delayed free recall of the brief 5‐item memory list contributes to widely used MoCA total scores, the optional cued recall and multiple‐choice recognition subtests may provide better diagnostic accuracy than free recall alone. Method Data on 719 individuals with Mild Cognitive Impairment and 601 cognitively unimpaired controls were obtained from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database. The Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (AVLT) delayed free recall condition was used to characterize level of memory performance. Participants with demographically adjusted T‐scores of ≤ 2 SDs below the mean were classified as ‘impaired.’ Binary logistic regressions assessed if combined MoCA cued/recognition performance was a significant predictor of impaired delayed recall on the AVLT beyond the contribution of free recall and while covarying for age, education, and gender. Sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratio values were also examined for the MoCA free recall and combined cued/recognition scores. Result Free recall on the MoCA was a significant predictor of delayed recall on the AVLT (b = ‐1.207, Wald χ2 (1) = 128.044, p < 0.001, OR = 0.299, 95%CI = [0.243, 0.369]. The addition of the combined MoCA cued recall/recognition conditions improved the overall model fit (χ2(1) = 30.616, p<.001) and predicted impaired AVLT recall such that for every additional word on combined MoCA cued recall/recognition, the likelihood of being in the AVLT memory impaired group decreased by 33% (b = ‐0.400, Wald χ2 (1) = 29.834, p < 0.001, OR = 0.670, 95%CI = [0. 581, 0.774]). Combined MoCA cued recall/recognition had both higher specificity and likelihood ratios in detecting AVLT memory impairment than MoCA free recall, while higher sensitivity values were present for MoCA free recall (see Table 1). Conclusion Use of combined cued/recognition memory conditions provides clinicians with improved diagnostic accuracy in detecting memory impairment. In settings where specificity in detecting memory impairment is important, administration of the MoCA free recall as well as cued recall and recognition conditions is recommended.

records.title: Enhanced memory for sentences read aloud conversationally versus clearly: Evidence from sentence recognition memory and recall
records.venue: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
records.abstract: Native and non-native listeners were more accurate in identifying sentences as previously heard and in recalling words and entire sentences when they heard clear speech compared to conversational speech (Keerstock and Smiljanic, 2018, 2019). This clear speech benefit on listeners' memory might in part be due to decreased listening effort in perceiving intelligibility-enhancing clear speech (“effortfulness hypothesis,” Rabbitt, 1968). The effect of reading sentences aloud in clear speech on talkers' memory, however, is unknown. We hypothesized that the effort required to produce clear speech could detrimentally affect memory encoding. In the present study, native and non-native English speakers read sentences aloud in clear and conversational speaking styles. Their memory of the read sentences was assessed either via a sentence recognition memory task (Experiment 1; n = 90) or a recall task (Experiment 2; n = 75). Results from both experiments showed superior retention of spoken information for sentences read aloud conversationally rather than clearly. The results indicate that producing clear speech, unlike perceiving it, interferes with sentence recognition memory and recall. Production of listener-oriented hyper-articulated speech may increase cognitive load leaving fewer cognitive resources available for storing spoken information in memory.

records.title: A Comparative Analysis of Psychometric Properties of Memory Tasks and Their Relationships with Higher-Order Thinking Skills: Recognition Versus Recall
records.abstract: This study aims to compare the psychometric properties of recognition and recall task measurements and to examine their relationships with other higher-order thinking skills. Memory measurements made with recognition and recall tasks were based on the Visual Span Memory (VSM) subtest of the ASIS intelligence scale. The participants of the study consisted of 228 students attending first and second grade in a primary school in the city center of Eskişehir. The data were collected by administering the recognition and recall task forms to the students individually. The findings reveal a statistically significant difference between the average scores of recall and recognition tasks. The mean scores of the recognition task measurements are significantly higher than the mean scores of the recall task measurements (t(227) = 5.79, p <0.01; Cohen d = 0.435, Cohen dz = 0.38). In addition, there is a significant difference between the reliability coefficients of recognition and recall task score in favor of the recall task score (χ2(1) = 6.181, p <.02). It was also found that the mean item-total correlations of the recall task measurements (r=.41) were higher than the recognition task measurements (r=.27), and the item-total correlations of the 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 11th, and 14th items differed significantly in favor of the recall task measurements. The correlation of the recall task score with the other 5 subtests in the ASIS intelligence scale was higher than that of the recognition task score. The findings show that the psychometric properties of the measurement performed with the recall task are stronger.

records.title: Clinical value of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment free recall condition alone versus cued recall and recognition conditions to detect true memory impairment
records.abstract: The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) is widely used as a screener to characterize cognition. Although only the delayed free recall condition is required for administration, performance on the optional cued recall and multiple-choice recognition conditions may improve diagnostic accuracy over free recall alone. Data on 719 individuals with MCI and 601 controls were obtained from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database. The Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (AVLT) delayed free recall condition was used as the gold standard of memory status. Participants with T-scores ≤30 (≤2 SDs below the mean) were classified as memory “impaired.” Binary logistic regressions assessed if combined MoCA cued recall/recognition predicted impaired delayed recall on the AVLT beyond the contribution of MoCA free recall. Results showed that MoCA free recall predicted AVLT delayed recall, and that the addition of combined MoCA cued recall/recognition improved the ability to detect impaired AVLT recall, with a better overall model fit. The combined MoCA cued recall/recognition score also had higher specificity and likelihood ratios in detecting memory impairment than MoCA free recall, while higher sensitivity values were present for free recall. Thus, the additional administration of the MoCA cued recall and recognition is recommended.

records.title: Recognition versus Recall
records.abstract: The issue of Recall versus Recognition is one of the oldest debates of advertising research according to experts like Alexander Biel. It started when Starch and Gallup introduced these measures in the 1930s. It became confused with other arguments after Schwerin introduced Persuasion measures into copy testing in the late 1940s. It was extended to left-brain/right-brain theories by Krugman and related specifically to his view of how print and TV advertising works, in the mid 1970s. Zielske extended the brain hemispheric theories to emotive/rational advertising in 1982. In the same year Gibson published his famous paper “Not Recall.” In 1992 John Rice renewed this argument based on hemispheric theories in South Africa.These are famous names, known to most researchers and advertisers. Few people have actually read what these authors really said, or critically inspected the empirical basis for their arguments. The fact is that there exists virtually no empirical evidence, nor consistency of views among these papers.This paper first reviews these papers in terms of their conclusions and empiricism. Then scientists' current views of brain hemispheric theories and of memory are reviewed. Finally, the results of three experiments conducted to examine comparative measures for Recall and Recognition, all on a larger scale than any of the previous experiments, are discussed.

records.title: PRESERVED RECALL VERSUS IMPAIRED RECOGNITION: A CASE STUDY
records.abstract: A very pure and most unusual case of memory impairment is reported in a patient operated on for an aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery. Neuropsychological investigation performed about 8 yrs after the operation revealed a dissociation between very poor performance on recognition tests (on which the patient's performance was as poor as that in classical amnesic patients) and normal performance (estimated by the number of correct responses) in recall. This pattern has not previously been reported and is the reverse of that observed both in normal subjects and in amnesic patients. In addition, the patient was able to achieve a number of difficult learning tasks, at times normally; the relearning of one of these tasks after a delay of 1 h was perfectly normal. The recognition failure is interpreted in terms of the suggestion that memory performance results from an interaction between knowledge and subjective experience of remembering.

records.title: B - 75 Recall Versus Recognition? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Recall Versus Recognition Testing to Differentiate Diagnostic Groups
records.abstract: Objective A systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the clinical utility of separate recall and recognition testing in the identification of anterograde memory impairment. Data Selection Articles published from 2010 onwards that reported outcomes for both recall and recognition testing in patients with a diagnosed memory disorder compared to community controls were eligible for inclusion. A search of PsycINFO, Medline, and EMBASE databases in June 2020 led to a total of 63 articles. Standardized mean differences between patients and controls were calculated for recall and recognition outcomes. Study quality was assessed using a modified QUADAS-2 form. Data Synthesis Multivariate meta-analyses revealed that overall, patients performed significantly worse than controls on both recall (Hedges’ g = 2.37, 95%CI: 1.88 to 2.87) and recognition tests (Hedges’ g = 1.62, 95%CI: 1.26 to 1.99). A comparison of effect sizes between recall and recognition outcomes using multivariate meta-analysis showed that recall tests were significantly more impaired in patients versus controls (g = 0.76, 95%CI: 0.54 to 0.98) across all test categories and all diagnostic categories, except temporal lobe epilepsy, likely due to the small sample size for this group. The results were not influenced by test material (i.e., verbal or visual), the age or education of patients, or studies considered to have a high risk of bias. Conclusions The results show that recall test scores provide a more effective method to identify anterograde memory impairment compared to recognition test scores, regardless of the underlying cause of memory impairment. In no diagnostic group examined did recognition testing confer any advantage.

records.title: BRIEF REPORT Bilinguals' recall and recognition of emotion words
records.abstract: Recall of emotion words is superior to neutral words. Prior work reported in this journal (Anooshian & Hertel, 1994) found that this effect was absent in a second language. Words in a second language may thus lack the emotional associations of words acquired in childhood. To determine whether memory probes may be generally useful for assessing emotionality effects in a first versus a second language, Anooshian and Hertel's paradigm was extended in several ways. Recall was compared to recognition, and a variety of types of emotion words were studied, including taboo terms, and phrases likely to be learned in childhood (reprimands). Superior memory for emotion words was obtained in both the recall and recognition tasks, but this occurred in both the first and second language and indeed was stronger, for some stimuli, in the second language. This suggests that, even for bilingual speakers who acquire their second late (after age 12), words in the second language retain rich emotional associations.

records.title: Involvement With the Media: Recall Versus Recognition of Election Information
records.abstract: This study shows how additional measures of “involvement” can help explain variance in individuals' knowledge of election information and looks at differences in two operational definitions of knowledge. Adult respondents in the Austin, Texas, area were interviewed by telephone in October 1986. The study partially supports Krugman's (1977) contention that knowledge derived from newspaper reading may be best tapped by recall-type questions that access left-brain processing, whereas knowledge derived from television viewing may be best tapped by recognition-type questions that access right-brain processing. Although in general television- and newspaper-reliant individuals scored equally well on the recognition test of election knowledge, the study also shows that younger, newspaper-reliant individuals recalled more than did younger, television-reliant respondents. This was not true of older respondents, however, suggesting that long-term memory may help fill in the blanks in left-brain processing that may be neglected among those who are television reliant. The issue should be directed away from whether information is retrievable through recall-type questions and toward whether it is retrievable in a way that will be useful in making political decisions.

records.title: Modeling hippocampal and neocortical contributions to recognition memory: A complementary-learning-systems approach.
records.abstract: The authors present a computational neural-network model of how the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe cortex (MTLC) contribute to recognition memory. The hippocampal component contributes by recalling studied details. The MTLC component cannot support recall, but one can extract a scalar familiarity signal from MTLC that tracks how well a test item matches studied items. The authors present simulations that establish key differences in the operating characteristics of the hippocampal-recall and MTLC-familiarity signals and identify several manipulations (e.g., target-lure similarity, interference) that differentially affect the 2 signals. They also use the model to address the stochastic relationship between recall and familiarity and the effects of partial versus complete hippocampal lesions on recognition.

records.title: Recall and recognition of brand names: A comparison of word and nonword name types
records.abstract: Despite the common recommendation that brand names be memorable, little is known about the effect of brand name type on various forms of memory processing such as recall and recognition. As such, this article extends prior research by comparing recall and recognition for three sets of brand names: words versus nonwords, relevant (i.e., related to a product attribute) words versus irrelevant (i.e., unrelated to a product attribute) words, and relevant words cuing an advertised attribute versus relevant words cuing an unadvertised attribute. The results of an experimental study indicate that memory for these brand name types depends on whether it is accessed via recall or recognition. Based on these results, implications for naming new products are discussed. © 2002 Wiley Periodicals, Inc.

records.title: Advertising Recognition and Recall by Age--Including Teens
records.abstract: Published information on memory for advertising as a function of age appears to be limited to younger (18 to 34) versus older adults (35+) and to the “day-after recall” measure. Additional data from three copytesting companies adds the brand recall and recognition measures to the literature—and adds data for teenagers. Memory for advertising is found to vary as a function of age across all three measures: For each measure, young adults remember advertising better than older adults, and teens remember advertising better than young adults.

records.title: Mixed- versus strong right-handedness is associated with biases towards "remember" versus "know" judgements in recognition memory: Role of interhemispheric interaction
records.abstract: Growing evidence supports the hypothesis that episodic versus semantic memories rely primarily on interhemispheric versus intrahemispheric processing, respectively. For example, a recent study found that individuals with presumed greater interhemispheric interaction were superior in episodic recall but inferior at semantic word fragment completion; however, tests of recognition memory yielded no group differences. Interestingly, recognition memory can be based on either explicitly remembering a stimulus or implicitly knowing that a stimulus had been presented. The current experiments administered recognition memory tests to strongly versus mixed handed participants who judged for each recognised item whether their response was based on remembering (episodic memory) or knowing (semantic memory) (Tulving, 1983). Results indicate that strong versus mixed handers are biased towards basing recognition responses on judgements of knowing versus remembering, respectively. As strong versus mixed handedness is associated with greater versus lesser interhemispheric processing, the results support the original hypothesis.

records.title: Recognition and Recall in Slow Movements: Separate Memory States?
records.abstract: If slow positioning movements are governed only by a recognition process (e.g., Schmidt, 1975) then subject's performance should be independent of the mode or response (active versus passive). Two groups learned a criterion movement under either active or passive conditions following which KR was withdrawn. Although no differences were apparent on acquisition trials, active-group performance deteriorated dramatically during KR withdrawal while passive-group performance remained stable. These results suggest that recall and recognition are potentially separable in slow movements on the basis of the information available to the performer.

records.title: Effects of organization on recognition memory.
records.abstract: The effect of organization on recognition memory was investigated in two experiments. In both experiments, a categorized list was presented for study with instances of a given category being either blocked or distributed randomly throughout the list. The order of items in the recognition test was of varied similarity to their order within the blocked study list. Results indicated that the effect of blocked versus random presentation tended to be dependent on the order of recognition test items. In the first experiment, blocked presentation enhanced recognition only when test items were grouped on the basis of category membership and the order of old items within a category was the same as it had been in the study list. A similar trend was observed in the second experiment. Results were discussed with reference to the role of retrieval in recognition memory. Tulving and Thomson (1971) have suggested that retention of an event, regardless of the type of test, is dependent on the storage of appropriate mnemonic information and the retrievability of that information at the time of test. In contrast, Kintsch (1970b) has suggested that a portion of the retrieval process, search, is involved only in tests of recall. The effect on recall of relationships between study items is attributed to an effect on search; interitem relationships are employed to aid in locating an item in memory. To support the claim that recognition does not involve a search process, recognition memory must be shown to be independent of interitem relationships. Differences in the effects of organizational variables on recall and on recognition have been observed. records.title: Why is free recall practice more effective than recognition practice for enhancing memory? Evaluating the relational processing hypothesis
The effect of semantic relatedness on immediate serial recall and serial recognition
records.abstract: The present study examined the effects of semantic relatedness on immediate serial recall and serial recognition. Each participant received either blocked or randomly intermixed serial recall or serial recognition trials. Replicating the findings of previous studies (e.g., Saint-Aubin, Ouellette, & Poirier, 2005), semantic relatedness boosted percentage serial recall but also increased order errors, after taking into account the proportion of correctly recalled items, regardless of their orders, in serial recall trials. In serial recognition trials, participants' responses were slower and less accurate for related lists than for unrelated lists. There were intraindividual correlations among order memory measures in serial recall versus serial recognition trials. The implications of these findings for item redintegration theories are discussed.

records.title: The role of emotion in recognition with versus without cued-recall
authors: Malcolm, Matthew P. (Matthew Paul), committee member
records.venue: Digital Collections of Colorado (Colorado State University)
records.abstract: In the present study, we sought to examine the effects of emotion on the processes that subserve recognition memory. Specifically, we explored how two primary dimensions of emotion (negative valence and high arousal) separately impact the two processes of recognition memory (recollection and familiarity). To separately examine recollection and familiarity, the recognition without cued-recall method was used to separate out judgments of recognition that are accompanied vs. unaccompanied by cued-recall. Data from three experiments suggest that both negative valence and high arousal increase both cued-recall performance itself and recognition accompanied by cued recall, without affecting the ability to recognize in the absence of cued-recall. Additionally, two emotional biases were found. The first bias, found in a within-subjects manipulation, involves an increase in recognition ratings for cues corresponding to unrecalled negative items relative to cues corresponding to unrecalled neutral items. The second bias was an increase in recognition ratings for cues corresponding to negative and arousing nonstudied items that were identified relative to cues corresponding to neutral nonstudied items that were identified.

records.title: Recognition is Easy; Recall is Hard
The Effect of Binaural Beats on Recognition and Recall
records.venue: Digital Commons - New Heaven (University of New Haven)
records.abstract: Binaural beats, the playing of a different frequency in each ear that the brain perceives as one, have been tested with recognition and recall in forms of simple memory tasks. However, there is a lack of investigation on binaural beats' effect on recognition and recall in more complicated ways of these forms. A relationship between these would be beneficial and additive to the field of music and memory as a significant effect could indicate a place in education for binaural beats. It is hypothesized that binaural beats will have a positive effect on higher forms of recognition and recall. Participants underwent binaural beat stimulation versus a no stimulation control condition and then completed a College Board PSAT Exam. The discussion of past methods of understanding music and memory can aid in the understanding of binaural beats' significance.

records.title: Non-Random Memory Recall, Selective Interpersonal Attraction, Reciprocal Devotee Synchronization, and Social-Media Visibility Governed by Hormonal Release Algorithms (V9)
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: This ninth version (V9) advances the Sarahu Neuro-Endocrine & Internal Determinism Framework by formalizing the principle that human memory recall, recurring or occasional thoughts about specific individuals, selective romantic/interpersonal attraction, charitable giving or refusal, jealousy, opposition, and public media recognition are non-random processes governed by hormonal release algorithms and mutual synchronization. In V9, whether a person or topic enters conscious recall—frequently or occasionally—and whether associated actions execute depends on the exact quantity of biochemical signaling released by hormonal algorithms at that moment. Drawing on a 100-subject observational study conducted at a Mutt (N = 100), V9 illustrates two foundational mechanisms: first, selective interpersonal preference (where a young woman dislikes one young man yet feels drawn to one among five candidates) reflects interpersonal hormonal algorithm synchronization rather than chance; second, fluctuations in devotee visits to the Mutt for guidance depend not on any deficit in the researcher's hormonal release, but on whether the devotees' own nervous systems release the corresponding biochemical signals prompting recall and movement toward the Mutt. Extending this reciprocal synchronization rule across daily social life, V9 accounts for selective charity versus refusal, public achievements, newspaper and television media coverage, jealousy, and opposition as non-accidental outcomes of aligned or misaligned hormonal algorithms.

records.title: Patterns of attentional and recognition-memory processing of emotional information among Chinese middle school students with different exercise volumes
records.abstract: BACKGROUND: Physical exercise is closely associated with adolescent mental health, yet emotional information processing among adolescents with different exercise volumes remains insufficiently understood. This study examined attentional and recognition-memory processing of positive and negative emotional information among middle school students with different exercise volumes. METHODS: Using convenience sampling, 300 copies of a modified 3-month-recall version of the Physical Activity Rating Scale-3 (PARS-3) were distributed at a middle school, yielding 291 valid questionnaires. In a cross-sectional extreme-group design, 60 students (30 per group) were recruited from the extreme ends of the high- and low-exercise-volume categories to complete the behavioral experiment. Task 1 used a dot-probe task to examine reaction time, probe congruency, and vigilance and disengagement/avoidance indices in response to positive and negative emotional pictures. Task 2 used a learning-recognition task to examine recognition accuracy, recognition sensitivity (d'), and response criterion (c) for positive and negative faces. RESULTS: In the dot-probe task, the Group × Valence interaction was significant, and the low-exercise-volume group responded faster to negative than to positive pictures. The Group × Valence interaction for the attentional disengagement/avoidance index was also significant, with the low-exercise-volume group showing a larger positive-picture disengagement/avoidance index, a pattern consistent with greater difficulty disengaging attention from positive pictures. In the learning-recognition task, Group × Valence interactions were significant for both d' and recognition accuracy, whereas the corresponding interaction for c was not significant. The low-exercise-volume group showed lower d' for positive than for negative faces, and its d' for positive faces was lower than that of the high-exercise-volume group; the accuracy analysis showed a corresponding within-group valence difference. CONCLUSIONS: Middle school students with different exercise volumes showed different valence-related patterns of emotional information processing, primarily in overall reaction time, the derived disengagement/avoidance index, and recognition sensitivity. Overall, exercise volume was associated with emotional information processing in adolescents. Because the behavioral sample was recruited from the extreme ends of the screening distribution, the observed group differences and effect sizes characterize selected extreme-group contrasts; they are not population-level estimates for typical high- versus low-exercise-volume adolescents. Longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to examine causal relationships.

records.title: Study on Multimodal Data- and Explainable AI-Based Risk Prediction and Intervention for Postpartum Depression in Nursing Care Settings
records.venue: Asia Pacific Journal of Clinical Medical Research
records.abstract: Objective: To evaluate a nursing-centered dynamic prediction and risk-stratified intervention system for postpartum depression (PPD) using multimodal longitudinal data and explainable artificial intelligence (AI). Methods: A quasi-experimental controlled study included 300 postpartum women enrolled within 6 hours after delivery and allocated by admission sequence to AI-assisted stratified nursing (n=150) or routine nursing care (n=150). Physiological, behavioral, psychological, and social-support indicators were collected, with EPDS assessments on postpartum days 7, 14, 28, and 42. A hybrid model combined temporal convolution, long short-term memory, text and voice representations, and multilayer fusion; SHAP and attention mechanisms supported case-level explanations. Outcomes included time to risk identification, EPDS trajectory, remission among high-risk women, nursing workload, and internally validated model performance. Results: Risk was identified earlier in the intervention group than in the control group (1.21 +/- 0.68 vs. 4.73 +/- 1.92 days, P<0.05). Mean EPDS reduction by day 42 was greater (-5.62 +/- 3.14 vs. -2.13 +/- 2.87, P<0.05), and remission was more frequent (78.3% vs. 42.6%; chi-square=36.41, P<0.05). High-risk identification reached 92.0% versus 64.0%. Time per follow-up decreased by 34.7%, and nurses reported fewer women requiring daily follow-up and lower work-related stress. The model achieved an AUC of 0.864, accuracy of 0.82, recall of 0.77, and F1-score of 0.79. Conclusion: A multimodal explainable AI system integrated with risk-stratified nursing care was associated with earlier risk recognition, improved depressive symptom trajectories, and lower nursing workload. External validation and a fully randomized multicenter evaluation are required before broad implementation.

records.title: Examining cognitive correlates of motivated memory in older adults using standard and naturalistic paradigms
records.abstract: Background: Learning and retaining information is essential for daily function. Research within several sectors of psychology (e.g., educational, cognitive, behavioral neuroscience) suggests that motivation and the reward system interact with memory structures, thus potentially influencing memory performance. This has been termed motivated memory. Motivated memory has been studied in adults across the lifespan but has yet to be thoroughly explored using established and novel, naturalistic paradigms in older adults. Studying the effect of motivation on memory in older adults is particularly important because a decline in cognitive function (i.e., memory) over time can lead to decreased independence and quality of life and an increase of caregiver burden. Motivated memory mechanisms may offer unique opportunities for intervention for those with cognitive decline. As such, greater understanding regarding the extent to which motivation can impact cognition, especially for memory for naturalistic, ecologically valid information, is needed. The aim of the current study is to gain a more thorough understanding of how motivation impacts memory. Specifically, we aimed to address important gaps in the literature regarding 1) the cognitive correlates of the motivated memory effect (i.e., episodic memory, executive function), 2) the type of information and learning processes that are most influenced by motivation (i.e., item memory, semantic memory, associative memory; free recall, recognition), 3) the effect of motivation on memory, specifically in a population of older adults, and 4) using a paradigm that simulates naturalistic information. Methods: This study recruited 53 participants to complete two cognitive tasks: an established task called the Selectivity Task (ST) and a novel task called the Motivated Memory Task (MMT). Both tasks assessed recall of higher value information compared to lower value information (e.g., motivated memory). Participants also completed questionnaires assessing their current mood, cognitive function, and motivation. The ST utilized an arbitrary point value system, and the MMT was designed to present naturalistic, health-related information that is of higher value (dementia risk factors and prevention facts) and lower value (polio risk factors and prevention facts). Participants also completed a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment, from which we derived composite scores of cognitive domains to examine cognitive correlates of motivated memory. Regressions examined the cognitive correlates of motivated memory on the ST, using the selectivity index (ST-SI; Aim 1). A series of ANCOVAs were performed to evaluate the effect of motivation on recalling higher versus lower value items on the novel MMT (Aim 2). Results: Results suggest that the ST-SI was not associated with either episodic memory, executive function, or motivation score. Contrary to our hypotheses, on the MMT, participants recalled more semantic details about the prevention facts for polio overall, across all time points. However, consistent with hypotheses, participants recognized dementia risk factors with greater accuracy than polio risk factors on a test of delayed recognition. Conclusion: Motivation to learn health information may influence item recognition memory but not free recall and not semantic or associative memory, possibly providing support for the dual-process theory of memory and aging. These results suggest that healthcare providers should encourage patients to use cue-based recognition for their care rather than relying on free recall.

records.title: Chronic Electroconvulsive Shock Disrupts Hippocampal Physiology and Impairs Associative Memory in Mice
records.abstract: Electroconvulsive therapy ( ECT ) is a highly effective treatment for depression but it has undesirable side effects on various aspects of cognition, including memory. Patients may display retrograde amnesia for autobiographical events and anterograde amnesia in tests of recall and recognition memory. These amnestic effects are likely to depend, at least in part, on changes in the hippocampus. ECT ‐induced volume increases in the hippocampus and dentate gyrus subregion in particular correlate with the cognitive deficits. However, the precise cellular and behavioral effects of ECT remain poorly understood. Here, we therefore subjected male and female mice to chronic electroconvulsive shock ( ECS ) and examined effects on hippocampal physiology and memory. Perforant path inputs onto dentate gyrus neurons were examined using whole cell patch clamp recordings in hippocampal slices. In the intact slice, perforant path stimulation did not result in any synaptic or spiking differences in mice given sham versus ECS treatments. However, GABA A blockade increased EPSPs and spiking in sham, but not ECS ‐treated, mice. Voltage clamp recordings further revealed weaker perforant path excitation of dentate gyrus neurons in ECS ‐treated mice. Extrapolating these findings to the intact animal, we then used Fos expression as a proxy for neural activity and found that ECS blunted exploration‐induced hippocampal activation, which was most pronounced in the dentate gyrus. Finally, recognition memory tasks revealed that ECS impaired memory for object‐context associations but not memory for objects or locations. Collectively, these experiments reveal that a clinically relevant schedule of ECS disrupts synaptic and circuit functions of the hippocampus and causes anterograde amnesia in a test of episodic‐like associative memory.

records.title: Misinformation resistance in memory reports of one instance of a repeated event: Post-warnings reduce misinformation endorsement in recognition
records.abstract: Previous research shows that remembering repeated events differs from remembering single events, yet little research has examined suggestibility in adults' memory for repeated events. In the present experiment, we investigated the effects of eyewitness misinformation and the role of a warning against misinformation in a repeated-event scenario. We examined how different types of misinformation - entirely new items versus items present in non-target instances - influence reporting. Three hundred and nine participants watched four surveillance-mission videos that shared a general story structure but differed in key details. Participants were later exposed to pieces of misinformation in a video narrative of someone else reporting the first mission. Reporting was measured using free recall, cued recall, and recognition. We replicated the standard misinformation effect in the repeated-event context. We found that the warning reduced misinformation reporting, but the effect was present only in the recognition task. Based on the source-monitoring framework, we expected it would be easier to resist external (entirely new) misinformation than misinformation consistent with what was present in non-target instances, and this was also true. The warning's lack of efficacy may be accounted for in two ways. First, the inherent difficulty of attributing details to specific instances of repeated events may have overshadowed the potential effects of the warning. Second, ours was a general warning; it might not have been strong enough to restore an adequate understanding of a memory task distorted by misinformation.

records.title: SPATIAL MEMORY IN AMNESIA - EVIDENCE FROM KORSAKOFF PATIENTS
records.abstract: Two experiments are reported which investigated a hypothesised disproportionate deficit in amnesic spatial memory. Korsakoff amnesic memory for the locations of objects or words placed on a grid was compared to control memory which had been attenuated by longer delays before testing. The effects of incidental versus intentional encoding of the locations were compared. No significant evidence of a disproportionate spatial memory deficit in Korsakoff amnesia was found, intentional instructions did not improve Korsakoff amnesic spatial memory scores, and there was no significant evidence of a trade-off of item memory and location memory specific to the Korsakoff amnesic group. Rather, intentional instructions significantly reduced item memory in both Korsakoff amnesics and normal controls, while having no effect on spatial memory. When location was scored by lenient criteria, there was no significant difference between groups for this measure, nor for recall and recognition memory for these items. Thus Korsakoff amnesic memory was very similar to that of control memory attenuated by longer delays before testing. The Korsakoff amnesic subjects' memory therefore differed quantitatively rather than qualitatively from that of control subjects' memory.

records.title: Have I Seen This Story Before? Multiple indices of memory after one year
records.abstract: Children’s memory improves markedly during early childhood. However, few studies track long-term retention for verifiable stimuli using multiple indicators. In this study, we followed 58 children (ages 5-8 years, M = 7.05) who had viewed six short, silent cartoons, narrated each story, and were tested for memory after one week (Hill et al., 2025). One year later, they viewed three repeated (“old”) and three novel (“new”) cartoons, judged whether each had been seen before, narrated each, and returned one week later for free and cued recall. Recognition of “old” versus “new” cartoons increased sharply with age: older children were nearly four times more likely to discriminate between old and new cartoons. In addition, narrative quality and free recall were higher for old cartoons, equally across age, indicating savings in relearning. To examine the basis of memory savings, we examined its relations with recognition of repetition, and enhanced narrative quality for old cartoons. Neither could explain age-invariant savings. Thus, young children retain complex, dynamic events after a one-year delay, as indexed by savings, while showing steady age-related change in free recall, and a qualitative age-related shift in conscious recognition of previous experience. Multiple indices of memory development are required for a complete portrait of the developmental trajectory.

records.title: Teaching Third Graders to Read Multisyllable Words: Segmentation Versus Whole Word Reading
records.venue: CUNY Academic Works (City University of New York)
records.abstract: In the early years of elementary school when children are still learning to read, they are presented with words of increased syllable length, and orthographic and morphological complexity in the texts they read. Although multisyllabic words comprise 90% of words in the English lexicon and carry important linguistic information for expanding vocabularies and comprehension of content, few studies have focused on teaching middle elementary children to read multisyllabic words. Many children lack strategies to identify these longer more complex words accurately and easily, leading to reading difficulties that place weaker readers at higher risk for school related problems and limit future academic achievement. Due to the importance of proficient word recognition of longer, complex words by the end of third grade, this study compared two methods for improving multisyllabic word reading: 1) segmentation of syllables and identification of morphemes, and 2) repeated reading of whole words. Sixty general education third graders, who did not exceed a third-grade-equivalent reading level, were randomly assigned to one of three conditions; Syllable Segmentation and Morpheme Identification, Whole Word Reading and Alphabetizing, or a No-Treatment Control condition. Students in the two treatment groups learned to read 80 multisyllabic words and their meanings over several learning trials. Two reading ability levels were distinguished to analyze the effects of the two conditions on better and poorer readers separately. Results compared both reading methods to business-as-usual classroom instruction. Based on developmental stage models of reading acquisition and phase theory of word recognition, superior effects of training in syllable and morpheme segmentation were expected across several literacy measures: multisyllabic word and non-word reading, spelling, and passage reading accuracy and comprehension. Results showed that both segmentation and whole word reading were effective at teaching third graders to read multisyllable words. This affirms the value of repeated practice reading words with corrective feedback to teach individual students to map pronunciations to different sized spelling units, including syllables, morphemes and whole words, to secure words in memory. On posttests the better readers in both conditions read the training words equally well and better than controls. However, the better readers in the syllable group outperformed better readers in the whole word group in remembering the spellings of trained words, in identifying affixes in trained words, in circling syllables in untrained words, and in reading multisyllabic non-words. The poorer readers in both groups made gains during training in learning to read multisyllabic words. However, the gains were greater in the whole word condition. On posttests, poorer reader in the two training conditions read training words equally well and much better than controls. However, the segmentation group identified more affixes than the whole word group. Poorer readers struggled to spell any words correctly but pretest to posttest gains recalling letters in the spellings revealed a difference favoring the two treatments over the control. Also, the segmentation group outperformed the control group in identifying base words and in reading multisyllabic non-words that contained morpheme subunits they had read in training words. Superior performance by both better and poorer readers who were taught to segment training words into morphemes indicates that they had consolidated these units during training and were using them to decode non-words. Although poorer readers showed some benefit from training, this instruction produced stronger effects in better readers, suggesting that this training may be more appropriate for readers who have acquired more substantial decoding skills, evidenced by performance at or above a 2.5 grade-equivalent word reading level. Results are interpreted to support orthographic mapping as a process that moves students into the consolidated phase in learning to read words.

records.title: Retrieval-Enhanced Suggestibility in Forensic Contexts: A meta-analysis of practice effects on eyewitness memory contamination
records.abstract: Retrieval practice can paradoxically increase vulnerability to subsequent misinformation, a phenomenon termed retrieval-enhanced suggestibility (RES), with implications for forensic interviewing protocols involving multiple recall attempts. This meta-analysis examines RES in forensic-relevant contexts and identifies boundary conditions moderating the effect. A systematic search identified 26 studies (k = 72 comparisons, N = 4 218) in simulated forensic contexts. Random-effects meta-analyses compared misinformation susceptibility following retrieval practice versus no practice, with moderator analyses (test format, misinformation source, detail type, retention interval, warning). Retrieval practice was associated with increased misinformation acceptance, d = 0.34, 95 % CI [0.23, 0.45], p < 0.001, I² = 56.4 %. Recognition-format tests showed larger RES (d = 0.66) than free recall (d = 0.17); narrative misinformation showed stronger RES (d = 0.48) than decontextualized question-based misinformation (d = -0.19); explicit warnings were associated with no detectable RES (d = -0.07, p = 0.41). In forensic-relevant experimental contexts, initial retrieval practice was associated with greater misinformation vulnerability, whereas free-recall formats, temporal separation, and explicit warnings were associated with reduced or absent effects. These findings inform the evidence base for forensic interview protocols.

records.title: Tunable Immune Imprinting of Memory B Cells to SARS-CoV-2 Variants 2255300
records.abstract: Introduction Immune imprinting, historically termed “original antigenic sin”, biases memory B cell (MBC) recall toward cross-reactive epitopes of ancestral strains, limiting vaccine adaptability to rapidly evolving variants. Whether immune imprinting is a fixed outcome of antigen exposure or can be modulated by host immune factors remains unclear. Chronic inflammatory and immunosuppressive conditions in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients affect antibody-secreting cell formation during MBC recall responses, but whether these host-intrinsic conditions can modulate MBC epitope targeting and immune imprinting in response to an antigenically distant variant remains unknown. Methods We recruited tightly time-matched cohorts of healthy individuals and SLE patients who had received three doses of ancestral inactivated vaccine and subsequently experienced synchronized Omicron BA.5/BF.7 breakthrough infection. We characterized their MBC responses through monoclonal antibody (mAb) epitope mapping, deep mutational scanning (DMS), spectral flow cytometry, and antigen-linked single-cell multi-omics. Results Healthy individuals displayed strong immune imprinting, characterized by robust recall of high-affinity cross-reactive MBCs. In contrast, SLE patients exhibited markedly reduced imprinting, with DMS revealing enhanced recognition of variant-specific neutralizing epitopes. Antigen-linked single-cell profiling showed attenuated MBC recall in SLE, associated with reduced MBC reactivation, diminished BCR signaling, and heightened inflammatory signatures. Concurrently, naïve and IgM MBCs were recruited and matured into variant-specific IgG MBCs, accompanied by a decline in early self- and polyreactivity. Conclusion Our findings demonstrate that immune imprinting in MBCs is plastic, and modulation of inflammatory and B cell activation signaling can rebalance recall versus de novo responses to promote variant-adaptable immunity. records.title: Evaluation of transfer learning by means of fuzzy logic for hand gesture recognition
MEMTIER: Tiered Retrieval, Session-Level Injection, and Typed Consolidation for Long-Running LLM Agents
records.abstract: Long-running large language model (LLM) agents accumulate memory across many sessions, yet most agent runtimes store it as flat text. We present MEMTIER, a tiered memory architecture and consolidation framework for an open-source agent runtime and study three questions: what to store, what to inject, and what to keep. First, a tiered episodic–semantic memory reaches an accuracy of 0.382 and an F1 of 0.412 on LongMemEval-S (N = 500) with a 7B model on a 6 GB GPU—a +33-point gain over no retrieval. A controlled single-pipeline ablation shows the gains come from two components—semantic pre-population and two-stage scoping—while the multi-signal retrieval scaffold is, in this setting, an operational pass-through of BM25 top-k; removing it entirely leaves accuracy unchanged. An oracle analysis explains why the system is retrieval-limited: on the diagnostic subset, the correct session is present in the candidate set 98% of the time, so the primary binding constraint is which evidence reaches the reader. A larger generator helps but does not remove the retrieval bottleneck. Second, the bottleneck is injection granularity, not session recall (90.9% session coverage versus 4.5% fact recall@2). Injecting all facts from the top-k retrieved sessions improves multi-session accuracy by +0.120 and knowledge update accuracy by +0.205, and a controlled comparison isolates a structure effect distinct from token quantity. Third, we cast memory consolidation as a Markov decision process, characterize three structural failure modes that render a learned policy uninformative on single-subject benchmarks, and show preliminary evidence on a live agent benchmark that a typed, keyword-based policy recovers near-oracle performance for one memory type (threat pattern memory) without supervision. Type-dependent retention for other memory types is proposed but not yet evaluated. We frame these as related diagnostic studies rather than a single validated pipeline, and, together, they cast agent memory as a pattern recognition problem: recognizing which session patterns carry evidence and which knowledge types to retain.

records.title: Memory performance, hippocampal volumes and memory fMRI in frontal versus temporal lobe epilepsy
records.abstract: PURPOSE: Patients with temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) and patients with frontal lobe epilepsy (FLE) show an increased risk of memory impairment relative to healthy controls, alongside structural and functional encoding-related cerebral alterations. To better specify syndrome-related differences, we directly compared TLE and FLE patients. METHODS: We evaluated 56 TLE (25 right-sided) and 24 FLE patients with respect to fMRI activation during encoding of scenes, faces, and words, post-scan recognition accuracy, neuropsychological verbal and figural memory tests, and hippocampal volumes. RESULTS: In the fMRI recognition paradigm, FLE patients were similarly impaired as both left- and right-sided TLE patients for scenes, faces and words. In contrast, on neuropsychological tasks involving multiple learning trials, we found a pattern of worse verbal recognition and delayed recall in left-sided TLE patients than in FLE patients, whereas right-sided TLE patients performed worse on figural recall. TLE patients also had smaller hippocampal volumes than FLE patients on the side of their seizure onset. For encoding-related hemodynamic activity, left-sided TLE patients showed lower left mesio-temporal lobe (mTL) activation during scene and face encoding than FLE patients. No group differences emerged in mTL activation during word encoding; however, FLE patients showed in tendency stronger right frontal activation than right-sided TLE patients. In addition, right-sided TLE patients showed weaker deactivation of the left middle temporal gyrus than FLE patients during face encoding. Default mode network analyses likewise indicated that weaker deactivation during the task is more marked in TLE than FLE patients. CONCLUSION: These findings reveal similarities but also underline task- and material-specific differences in memory performance and functional integrity between TLE and FLE.

records.title: Drawn to Light: Gendered Electricity and the Climate Unconscious in Yellowjackets
records.venue: ISLE Interdisciplinary Studies in Literature and Environment
records.abstract: Compared to other forms of energy consumption, electricity has long been either a symbol of technological progress and modernity, most recently in the coming transition to greener energy futures; or, contrarily, rarely considered at all because of its seeming invisibility in the background. In a marked contrast with early electricity users, contemporary use is characterized through a “magical relationship of invisible ease, of forgetfulness, of electricity without ‘seeking’” (Bakke 134; see Lieberman)—at least as long as the grid does not fail. This article draws on representations of electricity in a female-centered television series, Yellowjackets (2021–), where the stark contrast between the presence and absence of electrical power unfolds along gendered dimensions. We base our argument on understandings of electrical infrastructures, electricity consumption, or energy transitions as particularly gendered, racialized, and classed. In other words, discourses surrounding electricity are also discourses surrounding power relations and societal injustice. For example, the privilege of not needing to see or think about energy infrastructures and ignoring our vulnerable dependence on them is intrinsic to the Global North, while many worldwide live in a situation of “energy poverty.”1 When turning toward electricity as a guiding metaphor, we seek to explore what Sage Gerson describes as “the unjust cultural and imperial power relations that surround energy systems, [… as well as] the already disastrous impacts climate change has had on the power grid” (“Reading California’s Power Grid”; see Gerson, “Siphoning and Sabotage”). By foregrounding the conditions under which electricity can be taken for granted and those under which its fragility must be confronted, we explore a recent television series as unconscious reflection on climate crisis and the potential loss of energy infrastructures. Forms of energy consumption are rarely at the forefront of fictional television—and we do not argue that they should be—hence, the television series we turn to, Yellowjackets, is not a show about electricity in a narrow sense. Rather, we argue that focusing on electricity as an analytical lens enriches our understanding of popular culture and the gendered and ecological meanings it creates during the present era of climate change. We demonstrate how Yellowjackets links the presence and absence of electricity to the gendered vulnerabilities of the climate crisis, revealing television’s capacity to imagine alternative forms of collective survival in the form of the serialized hive. A tale of survival on two timelines, the female-centered series Yellowjackets intertwines two narrative threads: in one thread, in 1996, a plane carrying New Jersey’s champion high school girls’ soccer team crashes in the remote Canadian Rockies, leaving a group of teenage girls to survive nineteen months in the wilderness. The second story arc takes place in 2021 and introduces four survivors of this group, with each season serially expanding the cast by adding more survivors to both timelines. Despite their trauma and the media frenzy surrounding the disaster, the adult women attempt to continue their lives while concealing the exact circumstances of their survival. The show takes inspiration from controversial disaster stories that involved cannibalism, such as the nineteenth-century Donner Party in the Sierra Nevada mountains or the 1972 Andes Flight disaster, whose survivors included teenage rugby players from Uruguay. In viewer conversations and interviews with showrunners and actors, these historical events arise frequently, along with intertextual references to novels, TV series, and movies with survival themes.2 Yellowjackets is a fascinating case study because its primarily female cast and its almost instant feminist and queer cult status allow us to address how questions of gender matter in the energy humanities. From an ecofeminist perspective, this connection between energy and gender reveals how systems of power entwine environmental exploitation with the marginalization of women, particularly in the context of domestic labor and energy consumption. After all, “women do not appear very often in histories of energy, but when they do, their relation to energy seems very different than men’s” (Moore and Sandwell 4). Electrification especially has historically been heralded as liberating for women, promising ever more technological innovations with a seeming empowering impact for those in domestic care or reproductive work (see Sandwell 33). In addition to electricity’s promises for gendered notions of labor, leisure, and living, electrification has helped script new gendered energy identities—from domestic femininity to more authoritarian notions of masculinity. To conceptualize how gender politics are embedded in energy politics, Cara Daggett coins the notion of “petro-masculinity” to describe how “burning fossil fuels can come to function as a knowingly violent experience, a reassertion of white masculine power on an unruly planet that is perceived to be increasingly in need of violent, authoritarian order” (34). Recent aggressive reassertions of authoritarianism through fossil fuels compensate patriarchy in part by linking it to a perceived crisis of gender roles. Questions of how other gender formations relate to capitalist petrocultures follow from Daggett’s conceptualizations. Can there be an analogous petro-femininity invested in maintaining the fossil-consuming status quo or are female-identified bodies resigned to the status of mere commodities within neoliberal petrocultures? With its depictions of female-centered consumption of electricity—and the diametrically opposed position of the female consumer off the grid, stranded in the Canadian forest without electricity, Yellowjackets offers a revealing entry point into the question of how gendered energy identities are produced, negotiated, and contested. To investigate gendered discourses of electricity in television, we begin from the methodological starting point of the “unconscious” indebted to Fredric Jameson’s The Political Unconscious (1981), which we conceptually expand through Yellowjackets’s serially developed metaphor of the hive. Reworking the Freudian notion of the individual, Jameson argues that cultural and literary texts contain a complex, hidden ideological-political unconscious to be recovered through his Marxist aesthetic framework. Jameson’s work has been of interest to the environmental humanities, as evident in a series of reformulations of the concept: Lawrence Buell’s “environmental unconscious,” Patricia Yaeger’s “energy unconscious,” Roman Bartosch’s “petroleum unconscious,” Harry Pitt Scott’s “energopolitical unconscious,” Mark Bould’s “Anthropocene unconscious,” and Julia Leyda’s “climate unconscious.” Despite their differences, these conceptions share an interest in foregrounding the energy- and environment-related absences of a text that are central to its production and reception. This concept of the unconscious as a reading strategy and a theoretical lens is particularly helpful to explore the impact of climate crisis in screen culture and popular culture. As Leyda writes, “a widespread awareness of climate change worms its way into every form of media, to the extent that contact with media means it cannot be avoided” (5). Hence, this reading method informed by the environmental and energy humanities makes legible the changed viewing position of television audiences during times of climate change. Building upon such conceptualizations, we argue that electricity lends itself to an analysis of the climate unconscious because of how often it is understood as an invisible entity or force, specifically in a gendered way. Among the “sometimes surprising and banal ways” (Leyda and Negra 79) that practices of energy consumption and energy infrastructures manifest in television series are subtle, taken-for-granted aspects. For example, as we argue elsewhere, television shows may depict futures without air conditioning to signify changed climates and energy consumption (see Leyda, “Post-air-conditioning”) or highlight mobility and controversial air travel practices through frequent location changes (see Sulimma, “The Plane”). The following sections explore how Yellowjackets engages with electricity as a narrative and symbolic force. Each examines a distinct aspect—temporal and spatial dynamics related to electricity uses or absences in the different timelines, sources of light as a key interest of film and television studies, and the hive metaphor in connection to serial media—to trace how the show’s energy aesthetics reflect broader cultural climate imaginaries. Further, we extend notions of the climate unconscious through Yellowjackets’s swarm metaphor as a layered figure for collectivity, energy transfer, and decentralized networks.
